chapter: Other drummers and New Orleans musicians
title: Tambourine and sock cymbals on early kits
summary: They discuss the clamped-on tambourine and the low sock cymbal of early days.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: I'd like to hear you play on the tambourine on your drum. That would be interesting to hear that.

Well they used that just like a, looked like a tum tum too, you know, just hit licks on it. It's not. Hold it up in one hand or have it down? No, no, they had it, some kind of way they had it clamped on the side of the bass.
That might be a good novelty now. Yeah.
I was thinking of it myself, but getting the one. I tried.
Those heads are pretty thin, any danger of breaking the head if you hit on it with the stick flex?
Well I couldn't say because I never played none of them. I don't know just how hard the guys was hitting them. I used to see them hit them, but I don't know how hard they were hitting them.
They're not too easy to break, Bill. Not too easy, huh?
Mm-hmm. Hit on the rim and all too and make a lot of the jingle noise. Is there anything you can tell us about the drum sets and the way of when they began using the hi-hat or the sock cymbals?

Well the only thing I can say about that, Bill, is I had a chance to use one of the sock cymbals that they used during those days. It was a low-low cymbal. I said about this high up, what you would say, about a foot high. And the guys used to use that, but they never had a chance to use it. The two of those didn't work the stick on it at all? No, no, no, they didn't work the stick on it at all.
Frog, when you started, did you have a sock cymbal too in your outfit?
